report.summary: The alert is most likely a false positive. Event 1212797 is one small HTTP connection from a Windows 10 workstation (192.168.10.14) to the public address 144.76.121.172 on port 80. That address is not in the inventory and is not a known attacker. A search from 08:00 to 23:59 found only 7 connections to it, all between 19:13 and 19:33, each a few hundred bytes. That is far too little traffic to be a denial of service (DoS) attack. The connections come in pairs about every 10 minutes. That fits a routine update or telemetry check, but a weak beacon can't be ruled out. The detector's attack probability was low (0.0096) but above its very low threshold (0.00024). Neighbouring flows to the same host with near-identical features scored mostly below the threshold.

findings.statement: 192.168.10.14 is a private victim-LAN host, win10-pro-32 (Windows 10 Pro 32-bit). Its role is Workstation, its criticality is medium and it is not a known attacker.
144.76.121.172 is a public address. It has no asset record and no zone, and it is not flagged as a known attacker.
The anchor flow lasted 349 ms with 5 forward packets (791 bytes) and 4 backward packets (133 bytes). It had 2 SYN and 2 FIN flags and no RST.

Within ±15 minutes, 192.168.10.14 sent 1092 flows to 166 distinct IPs on 16 distinct ports. The top ports were 53 (562), 80 (293), 443 (205), 22 (14), 21 (4), 389 (3), 445 (2), and 135, 137 and 465 (1 each). Only 4 other flows went to 144.76.121.172:80, totalling 1863 bytes forward and 586 bytes backward.

A search from 2017-07-04 08:00 to 23:59 found 7 flows from 192.168.10.14 to 144.76.121.172, all on port 80. They fell between 19:13:32 and 19:33:11, in pairs at about 19:13, 19:23 and 19:33, roughly 10 minutes apart. Six flows had 133 backward bytes. The seventh, 1313331, had 187 backward bytes, 0 forward bytes and 1 RST.

The detector gave the anchor an attack probability of 0.0096, above the threshold of 0.00024. It predicted the dos family (0.59), with botnet second (0.40). The main features driving the score were Bwd Init Win Bytes = 241 and Subflow Bwd Bytes = 14.

Of the 4 neighbouring flows to the same destination, only 1238190 alerted (probability 0.00052, dos). The other three scored below the threshold, even though their traffic profiles are nearly the same.

A handful of small, completed request/response connections can't be a DoS. The near-identical flows score inconsistently around a very low threshold, which suggests a borderline score on harmless traffic.
Most of the source's traffic in the window goes to DNS and web ports, which likely reflects ordinary client activity. The few flows on ports 22, 21, 389 and 445 were not investigated further.

The 10-minute pairs with mostly fixed-size responses fit an automated client such as an updater or telemetry, and could in principle be a beacon. However, the host is not a known attacker and the volume is tiny, so benign polling is more likely.

recommended_actions.action: Close the alert as a false positive for DoS. Consider tuning the detector, because flows with near-identical features land on both sides of the 0.00024 threshold.
If host or proxy logs are available, check which process or URL on win10-pro-32 makes the 10-minute HTTP requests to 144.76.121.172, to rule out a beacon.

uncertainties: The flow records have no payload or HTTP details, so the application making the periodic requests to 144.76.121.172 can't be confirmed.
There is no external reputation data for 144.76.121.172; the local enrichment only shows it is not a known attacker.
Flows to 144.76.121.172 were seen only in a 20-minute stretch (7 flows). That is too little to firmly confirm or rule out beaconing.
The source's few flows on ports 22, 21, 389 and 445 in the window were not examined.

critic: The finding says the flows came "in pairs" at about 19:13, 19:23 and 19:33. The data shows three flows near 19:13 (1212797, 1238190, 1313331) and two each near 19:23 and 19:33, so the grouping is not a set of pairs.

report.summary: This alert looks like normal web browsing, not an attack. The detector scored it at about 1% attack probability. That only triggers an alert because the threshold is set very low, at about 0.024%. The source is win10-pro-32 (192.168.10.14), a Windows 10 workstation on the victim LAN. The destination, 144.76.121.172, is a public address that is not a known attacker. Over ±30 minutes there were only 7 small HTTP flows between the two hosts, with 133 or fewer bytes coming back per flow. The source's wider traffic is mostly DNS, HTTPS and HTTP to 321 addresses, which is typical for a workstation. There is nothing to suggest a DoS flood or a long-running stream of botnet check-ins to this server. Of the 7 flows, 2 cross the threshold and 5 don't.

findings.statement: The alerted flow 1212797 lasted about 350 ms and carried 5 packets / 791 bytes out and 4 packets / 133 bytes back. It closed normally (2 FIN flags, no RST). Over ±30 minutes the same source and destination pair had 6 other flows, all on port 80, totalling 3190 bytes out and 852 bytes back.

Over ±30 minutes, source 192.168.10.14 made 2652 flows to 321 addresses on 20 ports. Most were DNS on port 53 (1467), then 443 (599) and 80 (528). It received far more than it sent (about 33.3 MB in vs 1.7 MB out).
144.76.121.172 is a public address. It is not flagged as a known attacker and has no attacker notes or asset record.
192.168.10.14 is win10-pro-32, a Windows 10 Pro workstation in the victim_lan zone with medium criticality.

The detector scored the alerted flow at 0.0096 attack probability against a threshold of 0.00024, and labelled it dos (0.59) or botnet (0.40). Of the 7 flows between the pair, only 2 were above the threshold (1212797 and 1238190, at 0.0005). The rest scored between 1.8e-5 and 1.9e-4.

The traffic pattern doesn't fit a DoS attack: there are only a handful of short, normally closed connections with small byte counts. It also doesn't fit HTTP botnet check-ins to this server, since there are just 7 flows in an hour, the address isn't flagged and the source's other traffic looks like normal browsing. The alert is most likely caused by the very low threshold and by TCP window values in the flow that the model weighs heavily.

recommended_actions.action: Close as a false positive. Consider reviewing the detector's operating threshold, because flows at roughly 1% attack probability are producing alerts on ordinary workstation HTTP traffic.

If more alerts from win10-pro-32 point to 144.76.121.172 in other time windows, look up who owns the address and check whether the connections repeat at regular intervals (a sign of automated check-ins) before escalating.

uncertainties: There is no payload or HTTP content, so I couldn't directly rule out botnet command-and-control (C2) traffic over HTTP. The botnet family probability was 0.40.
I didn't analyse the exact timing between flows to this destination for a regular repeating pattern, only the counts and time range.
The local data has no reputation information for 144.76.121.172, so its ownership is unknown.
Part of the scoring output (E4) was truncated, so I didn't see the full result for event 1315194.

report.summary: This alert is most likely a false positive: ordinary web browsing from a Windows 10 workstation. Event 1212797 is one short outbound HTTP connection, not a long-lived one. The destination received only 6 flows in ±30 minutes, about 4 KB in total, all to port 80, so this is not a DoS burst. findings.statement: The anchor flow 192.168.10.14:57610 -> 144.76.121.172:80/TCP lasted 349.5 ms, sent 5 packets / 791 bytes and received 4 packets / 133 bytes, with 2 SYN and 2 FIN flags and no RST. This looks like a normal, complete short HTTP exchange.
Within ±30 minutes, the same source-destination pair had only 6 other flows, all to port 80, totalling 3190 bytes sent and 852 bytes received. That is not a flooding volume.

Within ±30 minutes, the source sent 2652 flows to 321 IPs on 20 ports, mostly DNS (1467), 443 (599) and 80 (528). It received about 33.3 MB and sent about 1.7 MB, a download-heavy pattern typical of a client.

The detector gives the anchor flow an attack probability of 0.0096, against an operating threshold of 0.00024. It labels the flow dos (0.587), with botnet close behind (0.405). recommended_actions.action: Close the alert as a false positive (benign outbound HTTP from a workstation). Consider reviewing the detector threshold, which makes probabilities below 1% alert on short web flows.
Optionally check proxy or DNS logs for the hostname behind 144.76.121.172 to confirm it is a legitimate website.

uncertainties: I have no payload or HTTP header data, so I could not confirm what was requested or which website it was.
I have no external reputation data for 144.76.121.172; only the local known-attacker list was checked.
The predict_attack output was cut off for the last flow of the pair (1315194), so I did not see its score.

report.summary: The detector rated event 3300170 at probability 0.276, which is far above its very low threshold of 0.00024, and labelled it dos at 0.82 (port_scan 0.18). The flow itself is tiny: 3 packets and 6 bytes forward, 4 packets and 14 bytes back, lasting 1.7 ms. It goes from 172.16.0.1, the firewall's NAT address that hides external sources, to FTP port 21 on web-server-16, a high-criticality host. The anchor has no SYN, but two FIN flags. It reuses source port 50833 from event 3096118 about two minutes earlier, so it looks like the closing tail of an existing FTP session. Over ±30 minutes this source sent only 29 flows, to 2 hosts and 3 ports (mostly 80 and 21). There were 8 small FTP sessions over about 25 minutes, each under 60 bytes. That does not fit DoS flooding, a port scan, or a high-rate brute-force burst. Neighbouring flows got mixed scores: 15 of 21 crossed the threshold, but with probabilities near 1e-3, and with both dos and port_scan labels. Because 172.16.0.1 carries all NAT'd external traffic, harmless and malicious traffic cannot be told apart by source address alone. The evidence does not support a confident true or false positive, so an analyst should decide.

findings.statement: Anchor flow 3300170: TCP from 172.16.0.1:50833 to 192.168.10.50:21. 3 packets / 6 bytes forward, 4 packets / 14 bytes back, 1.709 ms, 0 SYN, 2 FIN.
Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 29 flows to 2 destination IPs on 3 ports (80 x20, 21 x7, 0 x2). The pair with 192.168.10.50 totalled 27 flows, 9504 bytes forward and 27376 bytes back.

Between 19:11:40 and 19:36:03 there were 8 FTP flows from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:21. Gaps ranged from about 1 second (3300170 at 19:29:55 and 3186211 at 19:29:56) to several minutes. Each flow had 3–8 packets per direction, 6–14 bytes forward and 14–58 bytes back. Event 3096118 at 19:27:49 used the same source port 50833 as the anchor.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16: public web server, Ubuntu 16.04, high criticality, victim_lan zone, running HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. Its inventory notes list it as the target of FTP/SSH brute force, DoS, web attacks and DDoS.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside (NAT) address, flagged as a known attacker. Traffic from external attackers appears in the flow records under this source address.
The detector scored the anchor 0.276 against a threshold of 0.00024. Predicted family: dos 0.82, port_scan 0.18. The main contributing feature was Fwd Packet Length Max = 6.
Of 21 neighbouring same-pair flows, 15 were scored above threshold, mostly with low probabilities around 1e-3 and mixed labels (for example 3121434 and 3223757 as dos, 3124239 as port_scan).

The anchor looks like the closing tail of the FTP session in event 3096118 (same source port, FINs, no SYN). The overall low rate (8 FTP flows in about 25 minutes) and tiny volumes do not fit DoS flooding, a port scan, or a fast FTP brute force. The dos label is likely an artefact of small packet sizes.

recommended_actions.action: Have an analyst check the firewall NAT logs to find the real external source behind 172.16.0.1:50833 around 19:27–19:30 UTC, and compare it with known attacker addresses.
Review the FTP server logs on web-server-16 for 19:11–19:36 UTC (logins, failed authentications, commands) to decide whether these sessions were brute force, probing or harmless.
Do not escalate this as DoS. Volume and rate do not support flooding. Record that the detector's dos label on tiny FTP flows may be a false-positive pattern.

uncertainties: Because of NAT, the real external source behind 172.16.0.1 cannot be identified, so attacker and harmless traffic through the firewall cannot be separated.
No payloads or FTP application logs were available, so login attempts or their outcome could not be checked.
The prediction output was truncated, so not every neighbour's family and probability was reviewed.
No ATT&CK or CVE lookups were made because the observed pattern did not clearly match a specific technique or vulnerability.

report.summary: The alert is flow 3300170, a short FTP connection from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50 port 21 that the detector labelled dos. Around the alert the source made few connections to this host. In the ±5 minutes around it there were 8 flows, on ports 21 and 80 only. The search from 17:00 to 22:00 UTC matched 46 flows, the last at 19:48:03Z. The alerted flow is a tiny completed session: 3 packets carrying 6 bytes out, 4 packets carrying 14 bytes back, 1.7 ms. The source is the firewall's internal address. The enrichment notes say external attacker traffic shows up behind it after address translation (NAT), and the target is a high-criticality public web/FTP server. When the neighbouring flows were re-scored, 7 of 9 crossed the detector's very low threshold, but they were split between dos and port_scan. One more of the 9 did not alert at all. The evidence does not clearly show a DoS, but I can't rule out low-volume probing without payloads or a known-benign baseline, so a human should review it.

findings.statement: In the ±5 minutes around the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 8 flows, all to 192.168.10.50, on 2 ports (4 to port 21, 4 to port 80), with 2155 bytes forward and 7264 bytes back. The flows did not spread across many ports.
The alerted flow lasted 1.709 ms, with 3 forward packets carrying 6 bytes and 4 backward packets carrying 14 bytes. It had 2 FIN flags, no SYN and no RST.

A search from 17:00 to 22:00 UTC matched 46 flows from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50, from 17:00:31Z to 19:48:03Z. The earliest visible flows, from 17:00:31Z onward, were small connections with no payload bytes and a SYN and RST in each. They went to ports 80, 21, 22 and 444, plus repeated connections to port 443.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. Its criticality is high and it sits in the victim LAN.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's internal address and is marked as a known attacker. The notes say external attacker traffic appears with this address because of NAT.

The detector gave the alerted flow an attack probability of 0.276 against a threshold of 0.00024, with family dos at 0.82 and port_scan at 0.18. The biggest contributor was a small Fwd Packet Length Max of 6.

Of the 9 flows re-scored between the same two hosts, 7 crossed the threshold. Their predicted families were inconsistent: event 3305338 came out dos with probability 0.0007, while events 3345638 and 3096118 came out port_scan with probabilities 0.91 and 0.66. Event 3120154 did not alert.

The small flow counts, the completed tiny FTP session and the inconsistent family predictions do not clearly point to a DoS. The early SYN/RST connections to several service ports could be probing or health checks. Because the threshold is so low, a 0.28 score does not show much on its own.

recommended_actions.action: Have an analyst check whether the connections from behind the firewall's NAT to ports 21, 22, 80, 443 and 444 match a known monitoring or health-check source. Use firewall logs to find the real external source address behind 172.16.0.1.
Review the FTP server logs on web-server-16 around 19:29 UTC for login attempts or commands linked to this session.
Do not escalate this as a DoS incident on the current evidence: there are 8 flows on 2 ports in the ±5 minutes around the alert, and the re-scored flows give mixed families.

uncertainties: There are no payloads, so I can't see what the 6 forward bytes of the FTP session contained.
Because of the NAT, the real external source behind 172.16.0.1 is unknown, so this traffic can't be told apart from benign external traffic.
I didn't work out connection rates. The evidence gives counts and timestamps only.
Only part of the 5-hour flow search result was readable (it was truncated), so not all 46 flows were reviewed.
I didn't look up ATT&CK techniques because no attack pattern was confirmed.

report.summary: This is most likely a false positive. The alert is a single 1.7 ms flow, 6 bytes forward and 14 bytes back, from 172.16.0.1 to FTP port 21 on web-server-16 (192.168.10.50). It has no SYN and reuses source port 50833 from a flow two minutes earlier, so it looks like the closing tail of an earlier FTP session rather than a separate attack. In the full hour 19:00–20:00 the source made only 8 FTP flows to this server, each a few bytes and minutes apart. Across ±30 minutes it made 29 flows in total to 2 hosts on 3 ports. That is far too little for the 'dos' label, for a brute-force burst or for a port scan. The detector gave this flow 0.276. Its alert threshold is very low (0.00024), so it fires on 15 of the 21 neighbouring flows we scored, which points to an oversensitive model rather than a real attack. Some doubt remains: 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's NAT address, so attacker traffic and normal outside traffic both appear with it, and we cannot see payloads.

findings.statement: Anchor flow 3300170: 3 forward and 4 backward packets, 6 forward and 14 backward bytes, 1.709 ms long, 0 SYN, 2 FIN. It uses the same source port (50833) as flow 3096118 at 19:27:49.
Between 19:00 and 20:00, 172.16.0.1 made only 8 flows to 192.168.10.50:21 (19:11 to 19:36). Each carried 6–14 forward and 14–58 backward bytes.
Within ±30 minutes the source made 29 flows to 2 IPs on 3 ports: port 80 ×20, port 21 ×7, port 0 ×2. Flows between this pair totalled 9,504 forward and 27,376 backward bytes.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server (Ubuntu 16.04, criticality high) that runs FTP/21, HTTP/80 and SSH/22.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address. Traffic from outside, including the known attackers, appears with this address because of NAT.

The detector scored the anchor at 0.276 against a threshold of 0.000242 and predicted 'dos' (0.82) over 'port_scan' (0.18). Of 21 neighbouring flows scored, 15 were above the threshold, most of them with probabilities around 0.0005–0.0009.

The traffic pattern rules out DoS, FTP brute force and port scanning: the flows are few, small, spaced minutes apart and go to only 3 ports. The anchor looks like a session-teardown fragment. The tiny alert threshold explains why so many neighbouring flows also alert.

recommended_actions.action: Close as a likely false positive, after a quick check of the FTP server logs on web-server-16 for 19:11–19:36 UTC to confirm there were no failed-login bursts or unusual commands.
Review the detector's operating threshold (0.000242). It makes most low-volume flows from the NAT address alert.

uncertainties: 172.16.0.1 is a NAT address, so the original external source cannot be identified from the flows.
We have no payloads or FTP logs, so we cannot rule out low-rate, manual FTP interaction by an attacker.
The prediction output was truncated, so not every neighbouring flow's score was reviewed.
No ATT&CK lookup was done because the traffic did not match the suggested techniques.

critic: The 19:00 to 20:00 window is not in the summary or data of E5, which only gives first and last timestamps of 8 matched flows. The claim of 'only 8 flows' in that hour is also not backed: E1 shows the same pair with 7 port-21 flows over its ±30 min window, which does not match E5's 8.

report.summary: This looks like a false positive: an ordinary DNS lookup from a Windows 7 workstation to the internal DNS server and domain controller (dns-dc, 192.168.10.3). The flow was UDP/53 with 2 packets each way, 100 bytes sent and 356 bytes back, and it lasted 0.27 ms. Over the hour around the alert, the workstation's traffic was mostly DNS, HTTPS and HTTP, which fits normal use rather than a port scan. The detector scored 15 nearby flows from the same source and none crossed the threshold. The alert's own score (0.0084) is above the very low threshold (0.00024) but still low in absolute terms.

findings.statement: The alerted flow (event 4239790) was UDP from 192.168.10.9 to port 53 on 192.168.10.3. It had 2 packets each way, 100 bytes forward and 356 bytes back, lasted 0.27 ms, and carried no SYN, FIN or RST flags.

Between 192.168.10.9 and 192.168.10.3 there were 1,275 flows within ±30 minutes. 1,254 were to port 53. The rest went to 389 (7), 445 (4), 137 (3), 88 (2), 135 (2), 49666 (2) and 49671 (1), so 8 distinct destination ports in total.

The small number of non-DNS flows to dns-dc (LDAP, SMB, NetBIOS, Kerberos, RPC and high RPC ports) look like a workstation's normal Active Directory traffic. This is my interpretation of the port numbers, not something the tools stated.
Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.9 sent 2,755 flows to 397 IPs on only 19 ports. The top ports were 53 (1,254), 443 (960), 80 (475) and 8080 (29).
In the asset inventory, 192.168.10.3 is dns-dc, a critical Windows Server acting as DNS server and domain controller, with DNS/53 and Active Directory listed as known services.
192.168.10.9 is win7-pro, a private Windows 7 Pro workstation in the victim LAN. It is not a known attacker address.

The detector gave the alerted flow an attack probability of 0.0084 against a threshold of 0.00024 and labelled it port_scan. The biggest contributors were the forward length (100) and the backward minimum packet length (178).
The detector scored 15 neighbouring flows from 192.168.10.9 and none were above the threshold. The scores shown in the output were about 7.5e-06.

Lots of traffic to one DNS server plus wide spread over 443/80 matches a workstation browsing the web and resolving names. A scan would hit many ports on a few hosts, or many hosts on one probing port. The port_scan label probably comes from the packet-size features, not from scanning behaviour.

recommended_actions.action: Close as a false positive. Consider tuning the detector or suppressing alerts for small UDP/53 request-and-reply flows from internal workstations to the internal DNS server, given how low the threshold is.
Optionally, look at the DNS query names from 192.168.10.9 in DNS server logs to rule out DNS tunnelling or beaconing. The flow records here don't include payloads.

uncertainties: The flow records have no payloads or DNS query names, so DNS-based command-and-control or tunnelling can't be ruled out completely.
Only 15 neighbouring flows were rescored, and the detector output was truncated, so the full scores for every flow weren't seen.
The 397 destination IPs reached on 443/80 weren't checked one by one.

report.summary: This alert fired on one UDP/53 flow from the Windows 7 workstation win7-pro (192.168.10.9) to the internal DNS server and domain controller dns-dc (192.168.10.3). I'm closing it as a false positive. The detector scored it at 0.0084, which is above its very low threshold of 0.00024 but still small. In the hour around the alert, the workstation's traffic was mostly port 53 to dns-dc plus web traffic on ports 443 and 80, spread across only 19 ports. That doesn't look like a port scan. I rescored twelve nearby flows between the same two hosts and none of them alerted.

findings.statement: The anchor flow went from 192.168.10.9 to 192.168.10.3 on protocol 17 (UDP), port 53. It carried 2 packets and 100 bytes forward and 2 packets and 356 bytes back, lasted 0.27 ms, and had zero SYN, FIN and RST flags.
The anchor flow's size, duration and protocol match a normal DNS query and reply.

In the 30 minutes either side of the alert, 192.168.10.9 sent 2755 flows to 397 distinct IPs on only 19 distinct ports. The busiest ports were 53 (1254 flows), 443 (960) and 80 (475), and the total backward bytes were 31,648,869. Of its 1275 flows to 192.168.10.3, 1254 were on port 53. The rest were on ports 389 (7), 445 (4), 137 (3), 88 (2), 135 (2), 49666 (2) and 49671 (1).
192.168.10.3 is dns-dc, a Windows Server acting as DNS server and domain controller (services DNS/53 and Active Directory). It is rated critical and sits in the victim LAN.
192.168.10.9 is win7-pro, a Windows 7 Pro workstation rated medium criticality. It is a private address in the victim LAN and is not marked as a known attacker.

The detector gave the anchor flow an attack probability of 0.0084 against a threshold of 0.00024 and labelled it port_scan. The features that pushed the score up were Total Length of Fwd Packet = 100 and Bwd Packet Length Min = 178.
I rescored twelve nearby flows between the same two hosts (taken from the related-events sample, mostly port 53). All twelve scored about 7.5e-06, below the threshold, so none would alert.

This looks like a workstation resolving names through its domain DNS server and browsing the web. Many destination IPs on ports 443 and 80, few distinct ports and large return traffic point to browsing, not scanning. The alert is most likely a borderline score on a single flow.

recommended_actions.action: Close as a false positive. Consider tuning the detector, or suppressing alerts on routine UDP/53 traffic from victim-LAN workstations to dns-dc.

uncertainties: No payloads were available, so DNS misuse such as tunnelling can't be fully ruled out. The flow sizes look normal, though, and none of the nearby flows scored above the threshold.
Only 12 of the 1275 flows between these two hosts were rescored, and the result for the 12-flow batch was partly truncated. Its summary still says 0 of 12 were above the threshold.

critic: The finding says the anchor flow was 'in the 30 minutes either side of the alert', which is fine, but it also says the 1275 flows to 192.168.10.3 had 'the rest' on ports 389 (7), 445 (4), 137 (3), 88 (2), 135 (2), 49666 (2) and 49671 (1). Those counts sum to 1275 only if included, so this is supported. However the claim 'only 19 distinct ports' uses the word 'only', which is interpretation, not an observed fact.

report.summary: The detector flagged one UDP/53 flow from workstation win7-pro (192.168.10.9) to the internal DNS server and domain controller dns-dc (192.168.10.3) as a port scan. The probability was low (0.0084) but still above the very low threshold. The flow was 100 bytes out and 356 bytes back in 0.27 ms, which looks like an ordinary DNS lookup and answer. In the 30 minutes either side, the workstation's traffic matches normal use: about 1,254 DNS queries to its own DNS server, plus web traffic on ports 443 and 80. Neither host is a known attacker. Fifteen neighbouring flows from the same workstation all scored below the threshold. This looks like a one-off false positive on routine DNS traffic.

findings.statement: Anchor flow 4239790: UDP from 192.168.10.9:50493 to 192.168.10.3:53, 2 packets and 100 bytes out, 2 packets and 356 bytes back, 0.27 ms, no SYN, FIN or RST flags.

Within ±30 minutes there were 1,275 flows between the same two hosts. 1,254 of them went to port 53; the rest went to directory and Windows ports (389, 445, 137, 88, 135, 49666, 49671). Total 173,904 bytes out and 317,822 bytes back.
Within ±30 minutes the source sent 2,755 flows to 397 IPs on 19 ports. Most went to ports 53 (1,254), 443 (960) and 80 (475). It received 31.6 MB and sent 1.95 MB.

192.168.10.3 is dns-dc, the DNS server and domain controller (Windows Server), rated critical, in the victim LAN, with DNS/53 and Active Directory services. Within ±30 minutes it received 10,852 flows, 10,538 of them on port 53.
192.168.10.9 is a private address in the victim LAN. It is win7-pro, a Windows 7 Pro workstation rated medium, and it is not a known attacker.

The detector gave the anchor flow an attack probability of 0.0084 against a threshold of 0.00024 and labelled it port_scan. The main contributing features were packet-size features: 100 bytes total forward length and 178 bytes minimum backward packet length.
Fifteen neighbouring flows from 192.168.10.9 (DNS and others) were scored. All came out around 7.5e-06 and none crossed the threshold.

Many DNS queries to the domain's own DNS server plus lots of HTTP/HTTPS to many different IPs is what a workstation browsing the web looks like, not a port scan. findings.statement: 192.168.10.51 is ubuntu-server-12: a server running Ubuntu 12.04, criticality high, in the victim_lan zone, with an OpenSSL service on port 444. Its asset notes say a Heartbleed attack against port 444 on this host is scheduled.

All of them go to 192.168.10.51 on port 444 only, between 18:22:16 and 18:32:18 UTC, with 40,476 bytes forward and 33,127,315 bytes back in total. The anchor flow is reported separately: about 119 s long, with 2,796 forward packets totalling 7,920 bytes and 2,007 backward packets totalling 7,883,880 bytes.

CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed, CVSS 7.5) is an OpenSSL heartbeat buffer over-read that lets a remote attacker read process memory.

The detector's family label (web_attack) doesn't match the likely Heartbleed activity.

report.summary: This alert is very likely real attack traffic. The source, 172.16.0.1, is the firewall's inside address. External attacker traffic is translated (NAT) to this address, and enrichment flags it as a known attacker. The target is web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a public web server with high criticality, which the asset inventory names as a scheduled target of web attacks. The flagged flow is one long HTTP session: 34 s, 204 forward packets, 101 PSH-flagged forward data packets and about 72 KB sent back. It is part of 1,550 flows from the same source to the same server on port 80 within ±30 minutes. This looks like automated web attack tooling, such as login brute force or injection attempts that send many requests over one connection. There is no evidence that the attack succeeded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,550 flows, all to 192.168.10.50 on port 80 (one destination, one port). Together they carried 3,119,428 bytes forward and 6,365,767 bytes back. The server also received port 22 (127 flows) and port 21 (36 flows) traffic, plus single connections to many high ports, from senders other than 172.16.0.1.
The alerted flow lasted 34,020 ms, with 204 forward packets (43,906 bytes) and 105 backward packets (72,185 bytes), 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 0 RST.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16: a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22, high criticality, in the victim LAN zone. The inventory notes it as a target of the scheduled web attacks.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. External attacker traffic appears with this source address because of NAT.

The detector scored the alerted flow at 0.9994 attack probability, against a threshold of 0.00024, with web_attack at about 1.0. The biggest contributors were Fwd PSH Flags = 101, Down/Up Ratio, and Fwd Act Data Pkts = 101.
I rescored 20 sampled flows between the same two hosts. Only 1 of them crossed the alert threshold. Most were short flows with no backward payload and probabilities around 1e-5.

The alerted flow carried about 101 pushed request segments in one 34-second keep-alive session, and the source sent a steady stream of port-80 flows to a single server. That fits scripted web attack tooling, such as brute force or XSS/SQL injection, rather than a person browsing. Most of the neighbouring flows are tiny connection setups or teardowns, which explains why they score low.
172.16.0.1 contacted only 192.168.10.50:80 in the window, so this looks like a focused web attack rather than broad scanning.

recommended_actions.action: Check the web server and application logs on web-server-16 around 12:28–13:28 UTC for repeated login attempts, XSS or SQL injection payloads, and any successful authentication or unusual responses.
Use the firewall/NAT translation logs to find the real external source address behind 172.16.0.1, then block or rate-limit it.
Put a WAF or request rate limiting in front of the HTTP service on this high-criticality public web server.

uncertainties: The detector only sees flow features, not payloads, so I can't confirm the specific web attack type (brute force, XSS or SQL injection) or whether it worked.
Only 20 of the 1,550 neighbouring flows were rescored, and the output was cut off, so I couldn't see the full per-flow results.
I didn't look up a CVE because nothing identifies the web application or its version on 192.168.10.50.
Because of NAT, 172.16.0.1 may combine traffic from several external hosts.
